Probably not with unaided eyes.

Although the Moon is geometrically above the horizon, it is an **extremely thin crescent—only 1.53% illuminated—and just 14.2° from the Sun**. At the stated time it is also only about **13° high**, while the Sun is still **19° high**, producing bright daylight and strong atmospheric glare near the western horizon.

Under exceptionally transparent air, an experienced observer might conceivably detect such a crescent with optical aid, but for an ordinary observer using unaided vision the likelihood is **very low**. The Moon’s position only about **14° to the upper-right of the Sun** also makes searching with binoculars or a telescope hazardous while the Sun is above the horizon.

Your best chance would be shortly after sunset, when the sky darkens—but this Moon is likely to set soon after the Sun, so the viewing window would be brief and the crescent very low. Use a location with a completely unobstructed west-northwestern horizon.
